title: [Vantage Point] Maharlika’s billions: Where is the wealth being created?
summary: The Maharalika fund sits on substantial idle liquidity, an unresolved deployment pipeline, and the duty to prove the fund’s raison d'être

blocks.text: Has the creation of a separate sovereign investment institution made the country’s public capital more productive, or has it merely changed who manages it?
That is the question the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) — its outgoing leadership and incoming stewardship alike — must ultimately answer.

What does it truly take to turn P75 billion of public capital into a genuine sovereign wealth fund? It definitely takes far more than moving money across statutory accounts, incorporating an executive board, and announcing interim profits.

The real test has never been whether Maharlika can print accounting gains, but whether it produces economic value and risk-adjusted returns compelling enough to justify plucking those funds from the state institutions originally tasked with financing national development.
Three years in, that justification remains troubling to locate.

On the surface, MIC’s performance for the nine months ended September 2026 looks presentable. It reported P2.41 billion in gross revenue, P2.18 billion in net income, and P2.85 billion in comprehensive income. Yet a forensic breakdown reveals an underlying architecture that invites hard questions rather than celebration.

Of that P2.41-billion top line, P1.65 billion — nearly 69% — was generated simply from interest on liquid funds parked in banks and short-term placements. Only P756.5 million came from actual deployed investments.

Preserving capital while vetting transactions is sound fiduciary practice; reckless disbursement just to hit optics-driven targets would be worse. But the Republic did not establish a sovereign wealth vehicle to run an expensive treasury desk. If seven out of ten pesos earned stem from cash deposits, why establish an entirely new corporate machinery to capture standard deposit yields that government financial institutions were already equipped to collect?
The balance sheet deepens the puzzle.
As of September 30, Maharlika held P53.67 billion in cash and cash equivalents against cumulative capital deployments of P24.70 billion. More striking is the little that has been deployed.
A massive P15 billion, roughly 61% of disclosed cumulative investments, went into a single working-capital credit facility for Petron Corporation.

Petron’s role as the country’s lone crude refiner is undisputed, and underwriting energy security fits statutory mandates. But legality and systemic importance are merely the opening lines of credit analysis.

The revolving loan generated P343.4 million in interest over the nine-month period. What remains hidden, however, are the precise lending spreads, collateral cover, debt covenants, and single-borrower risk premiums.

There is a profound qualitative difference between catalytic development capital — funding high-risk, greenfield public goods that commercial banks shun — and extending short-term working capital to an established conglomerate that easily commands commercial credit lines.
If MIC merely replicates private syndicates, what incremental economic productivity has public capital achieved?

Other portfolio components reveal equal complexity. Equity participation in Asian Terminals delivered P292.7 million in recognized earnings and P368 million in received cash dividends — a concrete, realized distribution from a stable port operator.
Yet equity exposure cuts both ways.

In the third quarter alone, Maharlika recorded P941 million in net income, but its comprehensive income shrank to P157.9 million. That gap reflected roughly P783.1 million in unrealized mark-to-market losses tied to fluctuating share prices in Synergy Grid & Development Phils. Inc. Market swings do not necessarily indicate permanent impairment.
A sovereign fund, however, cannot tout paper gains as evidence of strategic genius during upswings, only to dismiss paper losses as irrelevant noise when the tape turns red.

MIC’s November 5 decision to shelve an additional investment in Synergy Grid shows healthy risk discipline. Turning away from a deteriorating deal is far better than burning state resources. Still, it leaves hanging questions: What valuation framework justified the original entry? What projected internal rate of return remains? How much downside exposure does the public carry?
This brings us to the root issue: opportunity cost.

Maharlika’s initial P75-billion paid-in capital was carved from P50 billion from the Land Bank of the Philippines (LandBank) and P25 billion from the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP), while the national government’s P50-billion balance remains unremitted.

Those were never idle balances. LandBank underwrites agrarian reform, farmers, and rural cooperatives. DBP finances roads, municipal water, public hospitals, and regional industry. Both operate under rigid capital adequacy ratios. Excising P75 billion in core equity from their ledgers inevitably diminished their credit-creation capacity.

The proper benchmark is whether Maharlika’s net returns — after factoring in operating expenses, origination costs, and single-asset risks — outperform the developmental lending multiples and steady statutory yields LandBank and DBP would have generated had they retained that balance-sheet power.

Progress has occurred: active investments accounted for 31% of total nine-month revenue, up from 3% in 2025. But execution has stalled. Management deployed zero new capital in the entire third quarter and conceded that its P35-billion target for 2026 will be missed.

As Rafael Consing Jr. departs the MIC executive suite on November 23, the looming leadership turnover should strip away public relations veneers. His successor will be bequeathed substantial idle liquidity, an unresolved deployment pipeline, and the duty to prove the fund’s raison d’être. (READ: The Maharlika fund that Joel Consing leaves behind)
The Philippine government did not need an entirely new bureaucratic apparatus simply to discover that P75 billion parked in bank accounts yields interest.

Until audited numbers prove that Maharlika creates tangible wealth, crowds in foreign capital, and expands the real economy beyond what existing public banks were already doing, the public is left with a sobering verdict: capital productivity has not been improved, and that what merely changed is who sits in the manager’s chair.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

This analysis draws from Maharlika Investment Corporation’s official financial disclosures for the nine months ended September 30, 2026; its announcements concerning the P15-billion Petron credit facility and Synergy Grid investment; Republic Act No. 11954, or the Maharlika Investment Fund Act; and contemporaneous financial reporting on management’s November 5 briefing, including Asian Terminals’ dividend contributions, unrealized investment losses and capital deployment targets. Financial assessments and conclusions are based on these disclosures, with reported figures distinguished from independently verified results.
